Both films are in conversation with one another; one rooted in history, the other in myth, each fascinated by the aftermath of world-altering decisions and whether redemption can be achieved. \n\nI love Christopher Nolan\u2019s The Odyssey; a sweeping, soul-stirring, elemental epic rooted in one of civilization\u2019s oldest texts yet told with a pulse that\u2019s distinctly modern and urgent. Every decision Nolan makes is in service of both scale and intimacy, emphasizing that behind the legend is a man reckoning with the cost of war, an insatiable longing for home, and the existential obligations that continue to define him.\n\nIt\u2019s impossible to overstate just how in lockstep Christopher Nolan, cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, editor Jennifer Lame, and composer Ludwig G\u00f6ransson are with each other. Together they\u2019ve forged a cinematic language that\u2019s immediately recognizable, culminating in two of the century\u2019s defining achievements within just five years.\n\nThe Odyssey is episodic, detailing key events of Odysseus\u2019s cunning invasion of Troy and the many hurdles he and his men faced finding their way home. Nolan leans into both horror and loss in equal measures; their encounter with the Laestrygonians specifically underscores the futility and heartbreak of their journey. Did tears fall watching Odysseus helplessly witness the men he left behind get torn to shreds? Well, yes! And Circe\u2019s sequence was an audacious swing into body horror that has me once again pining for Nolan to make a full-bore entry into the genre. \n\nAs far as performances go, it\u2019s a colossal ensemble effort led by commanding turns from Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Himesh Patel and John Leguizamo. I was also deeply moved by Samantha Morton, Zendaya and Elliot Page\u2019s limited yet profoundly impactful appearances. \n\nI suspect, much like Oppenheimer, The Odyssey will deepen over time.
